# Alternating current, transformer and power grid (`alternating_current_grid`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: needs dynamo_electric_motor, ohms_law_circuits; helped by water_turbine, steam_turbine, trigonometry
- Core idea: At a given transmitted power, the power lost in a line is current squared times resistance, so power should travel at high voltage and small current: ten times the voltage means one hundredth of the loss. A transformer makes this possible with alternating current: two coils on a closed core of thin iron sheets, where the voltages are approximately in the ratio of the numbers of turns. A generator without commutator gives alternating current at about 50 or 60 complete cycles per second; it is stepped up to thousands of volts for the line and down to about 100 to 240 volts for use. Three windings set 120 degrees apart give three-phase current on three wires, which produces a rotating magnetic field that drives simple motors without brushes (induction motor).
- Pitfalls:
  - Trying to transform direct current; a transformer works only with changing current and burns out on direct current
  - A solid iron transformer core, or a core that is not closed, which wastes most of the power as heat
  - Underrating the danger: high-voltage alternating current kills, so lines need earthing, fuses, insulation and distance
  - Connecting two generators without matching frequency and phase
  - Telling the story as Tesla alone against Edison; the transformer and three-phase system were mainly worked out in Hungary, Italy and Germany
- History: europe: 1831 – Faraday's induction ring; 1882–1884 Gaulard and Gibbs' series transformer system; 1885 closed-core transformer and parallel distribution (Zipernowsky, Bláthy and Déri, Ganz works, Budapest); 1885–1888 Ferraris, rotating field; 1889–1891 Dolivo-Dobrovolsky's three-phase motor and the Lauffen–Frankfurt line, 175 km at about 15,000 volts; americas: 1886 – Stanley's transformer system at Great Barrington for Westinghouse; 1887–1888 Tesla's polyphase motor patents; 1895–1896 Niagara Falls power station supplies Buffalo
- Read:
  - Thomas P. Hughes, Networks of Power: Electrification in Western Society, 1880–1930 (1983)
  - Jill Jonnes, Empires of Light: Edison, Tesla, Westinghouse, and the Race to Electrify the World (2003)
